newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban, allies take foes' strongholds.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban, allies take foes' strongholds.

text.p: Islamic Taleban warriors and their new-found Uzbek allies swept almost unopposed into the north Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Saturday in a startling collapse of opposition resistance.
Flying their trade-mark white flag over their tanks, they fanned out yelling "Allah-o-Akbar" -- "God is Great" -- to tear down portraits of opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Taleban sources said the purist Islamic militia and their allies had in the same day captured Dostum's military headquarters and main air base the northern town of Shibarghan after a mutiny in his small air force.
There was no word on the whereabouts of Dostum, whose mainly ethnic Uzbek troops had controlled northern Afghanistan since 1992.
Rapid setbacks of the past six days appeared to have reduced areas in opposition control to isolated regions in the mountainous north-eastern and central provinces.
The Taleban, which began as an Islamic student movement, already controlled the capital Kabul and most of the rest of Afghanistan, where it has enforced strict Islamic codes of dress and behaviour.

Afghanistan has hardly known peace in 20 years. The conflict began with Moslem guerrilla resistance to a communist government in Kabul, climaxed with the humiliating defeat of forces sent in by the Soviet Union and has sputtered on for seven more years as victorious guerrillas fought over the spoils.

The Taleban fighters rolled into Mazar-i-Sharif at about 5 p.m. on Saturday, firing assault rifles and rocket-propelled grenades into the air to celebrate their lightning advance through Dostum's heartland.
They arrived along with their new allies, Uzbek troops whose leader, General Abdul Malik, launched a mutiny against Dostum in the north-western province of Faryab on Monday.
Groups of civilian men watched silently as the city's conquerors made rounds.
Panic had gripped Mazar-i-Sharif couple of hours before as news spread that the Taleban and Malik's troops had seized Shibarghan, 130 km (80 miles) to the west.
Shopkeepers pulled down their shutters for fear of looting and soldiers ran for their tanks or commandeered private cars and taxis at gun point.

Civilian security men roughed up foreign cameramen, but none was seriously hurt. The streets emptied as people raced for their homes. Some were said to be trying to flee the city northwards towards the Uzbekistan border town of Termez, about 90 km (56 miles) away.
Witnesses said one of Dostum's generals received a telephone call at his office and then raced downstairs to his vehicle, shouting "It's all over".
Travellers from Shibarghan said they had seen several wounded Taleban soldiers arriving there on Saturday morning, apparently after clashes near Andkhui to the northwest.
Sources in the Taleban Islamic movement, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, that thousands of Dostum's troops in Shibarghan had been arrested while the rest had fled.
Earlier, three jet fighters of Dostum's air force defected to his opponents, a defecting officer said.
The Afghan Islamic Press agency also said defectors later flew another jet and two helicopters to the Taleban side.

A defecting officer of Dostum's air force, Major General Yussef Shah, told reporters in Kabul he made the 35-minute flight in his L39 Albatross trainer from Shibarghan airport because he feared that Dostum was trying to split Afghanistan.
Two Soviet-built Su-22 fighter bombers were earlier flown from Shibarghan to Maimana, capital of Faryab province, he said.
"We feared that Dostum was trying to dismantle Afghanistan. More planes are expected to come over," said Yussef, clean-shaven and wearing combat fatigues.
"One of the pilots was Colonel General Hafeez, the head of (Dostum's) air force. They bombed Shibarghan air base on their way out."
